title: The Untold Story Behind Barabbas
paragraphs: The Untold Story Behind Barabbas
There are moments in Scripture so brief that most people read past them without realizing they are standing in front of something terrifyingly profound.
Barabbas is one of those moments.
A criminal. A rebel. A murderer. A man whose name appears for only a few verses.
And yet his story may be one of the clearest human pictures of the Gospel ever recorded.
Because on the darkest day in human history… Barabbas watched Jesus Christ take his place.
Not symbolically. Not poetically. Literally.
One man guilty. One man innocent. One man deserving death. One man carrying the cross instead.
Most believers know the scene. Few truly stop long enough to feel the weight of it.

The crowds are screaming. Pilate is panicking. Religious leaders are manipulating. Roman soldiers are waiting. And standing somewhere in the middle of the chaos is a man who fully expected to die that day.
Barabbas.
The Gospel writers mention him in all four Gospels:
That alone should make us pay attention.
Scripture rarely repeats details without purpose.
The name “Barabbas” itself is deeply revealing.
In Aramaic:
“Bar” (בר) means “son.” “Abba” (אבא) means “father.”
Bar-Abbas literally means:
“Son of the father.”
That detail changes everything.
Some ancient manuscripts of Matthew even preserve his full name as:
“Jesus Barabbas.”
In Greek manuscripts:
Ἰησοῦν Βαραββᾶν (Iēsoun Barabban)
Meaning:
“Jesus, son of the father.”
Now pause and feel the collision happening in the courtroom.
Pilate stands before the people presenting two men.
Jesus Barabbas. A violent rebel. A false son. A guilty man.
And Jesus called the Christ. The true Son of the Father. The innocent Lamb of God.
Matthew 27:17 records Pilate asking:
“Whom do you want me to release for you: Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?”
In Greek:
Τίνα θέλετε ἀπολύσω ὑμῖν; Ἰησοῦν τὸν Βαραββᾶν ἢ Ἰησοῦν τὸν λεγόμενον Χριστόν;
The crowd had a choice between two “sons.”
One represented rebellion. One represented redemption.
One took life. One gave His life.
And humanity chose the wrong one.
That was not an accident.
It was a mirror.
The Gospels describe Barabbas as more than a petty criminal.
Mark 15:7 says:
“There was one called Barabbas, chained with his fellow rebels; they had committed murder in the rebellion.”
The Greek word used for rebellion is:
στάσις (stasis)
Meaning insurrection, revolt, uprising.
Barabbas was likely involved in violent nationalist rebellion against Rome.
John 18:40 calls him a “robber,” but the Greek word is:
λῃστής (lēstēs)
This does not merely mean a thief.
It was often used for violent revolutionaries, bandits, and militant insurgents.
The same word is used for the criminals crucified beside Jesus.
Barabbas was not misunderstood. He was not falsely accused. He was guilty.
Rome did not crucify people for small offenses.
Crucifixion was reserved for slaves, rebels, traitors, and enemies of the empire.
Barabbas was waiting for execution because Rome believed he deserved death.
And honestly? He did.
That is what makes the story unbearable.
Imagine the sounds of that morning.
Chains scraping stone. Roman boots echoing through corridors. Distant screams from crowds gathering outside.
Barabbas likely woke believing these were his final hours alive.
He may have heard preparations for crucifixions. He may have expected soldiers to drag him toward Golgotha. He may have mentally rehearsed his death all night.
Then suddenly… everything changes.
The cell opens.
A Roman guard speaks his name.
But instead of execution… release.
Matthew 27:26 says:
“Then he released Barabbas to them, but after having Jesus flogged, he handed Him over to be crucified.”
The Greek word for released is:
ἀπέλυσεν (apelysen)
To set free. Dismiss. Release from custody.
Barabbas walked out alive because Jesus walked toward the cross.
The innocent was condemned so the guilty could go free.
This is not hidden symbolism added later by theologians.
This is the literal historical scene.
Barabbas deserved the cross. Jesus took it.
That is the Gospel.
Isaiah prophesied this centuries earlier.
Isaiah 53:5:
“But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities.”
In Hebrew:
וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ (vehu mecholal mip’sha’einu)
“He was pierced because of our rebellion.”
The Hebrew word:
פֶּשַׁע (pesha)
Means rebellion, transgression, revolt.
Barabbas embodied rebellion. So do we.
Most people read themselves into Scripture as David defeating giants. Few realize they are Barabbas standing guilty before God.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
In Greek:
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον (pantes gar hēmarton)
“All have sinned.”
Not some. All.
The tragedy of humanity is not merely that we make mistakes. It is that we rebel against God while convincing ourselves we are good.
Barabbas knew he was guilty. Modern humanity often does not.
That may actually make us more spiritually blind than he was.
There is another detail many overlook.
The crowd screamed for Barabbas.
Luke 23:18:
“Away with this man, and release for us Barabbas!”
In Greek:
Αἶρε τοῦτον, ἀπόλυσον δὲ ἡμῖν τὸν Βαραββᾶν
“Away with this one! Release Barabbas to us!”
The same humanity that rejected the sinless Son of God embraced a violent rebel instead.
That spirit still exists today.
People still prefer false messiahs over true surrender.
We still choose pride over repentance. We still choose self-rule over holiness. We still choose rebellion over obedience.
The Barabbas story is not ancient history. It is human nature exposed.
But there is something even deeper hidden beneath the surface.
Barabbas disappears after his release.
Scripture never tells us what happened next.

Did he vanish into the crowd? Did he watch the crucifixion from a distance? Did he hear the hammer strike nails into wood meant for him? Did he spend the rest of his life haunted by the face of the man who died instead?
The Bible remains silent.
And maybe that silence is intentional.
Because now the story turns toward us.
What do you do after someone dies in your place?
That is the question Barabbas leaves hanging over every human soul.
Some scholars believe Barabbas may have eventually become a follower of Christ. Scripture does not confirm this. But imagine trying to forget the man who carried your cross.
Imagine hearing later:
“He rose from the dead.”
Imagine realizing the innocent man Rome crucified instead of you was actually the Son of God.
Imagine remembering His bleeding face every night afterward.
There is a reason this scene has haunted Christians for centuries.
Because Barabbas is us.
We are the guilty ones. We are the rebels. We are the spiritually violent. We are the lawbreakers.
And yet Jesus stepped forward willingly.
John 10:18 records Jesus saying:
“No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord.”
In Greek:
ἐγὼ τίθημι αὐτὴν ἀπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ
“I lay it down Myself.”
Jesus was not trapped. He was surrendering.
The cross was not a tragic accident. It was divine substitution.
Second Corinthians 5:21 says:
“For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.”
In Greek:
τὸν μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν
“The One who knew no sin.”
Jesus took the punishment of the guilty while remaining innocent Himself.
Barabbas physically experienced what every believer experiences spiritually.
Condemned. Then released because another took the sentence.
This is why the Gospel is not self-improvement. It is rescue.
Not advice. A substitution.
Not moral inspiration. A Savior standing in the place of the condemned.
Religion says: “Try harder.”
The cross says: “You could never save yourself.”
The story of Barabbas destroys human pride.
Because what contribution did Barabbas make to his salvation?
Nothing.
He did not negotiate. He did not earn mercy. He did not compensate Rome. He did not deserve release.
Grace interrupted his execution.
Ephesians 2:8 says:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith.”
In Greek:
χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι
“By grace you have been saved.”
Grace.
Unearned mercy. Unmerited favor. Undeserved release.
Barabbas walked free while Christ carried the crossbeam.
And somewhere between the prison and Golgotha is the entire message of Christianity.
The innocent Son of the Father traded places with guilty sons and daughters of rebellion.
That is why Jesus came.
Not merely to inspire humanity. Not merely to teach morality. Not merely to perform miracles.
He came to become the substitute.
The Lamb. The sacrifice. The atonement.
The Gospel becomes personal when you finally stop reading the Barabbas story as someone else’s testimony.
You are Barabbas.
I am Barabbas.
Every liar. Every addict. Every proud heart. Every hidden sinner. Every hypocrite. Every wounded soul. Every secret rebellion.
And still Christ stepped forward.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
In Greek:
ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν
“While we were still sinners.”
Not after we cleaned ourselves up. Not after we became worthy. Not after we fixed our lives.
While guilty.
That is the scandal of grace.
And maybe the most haunting question is this:
Did Barabbas ever look back?
Did he ever stand at a distance watching three crosses rise into the sky?
One cross originally prepared for him.
One Savior dying under his sentence.
One moment forever proving that God’s mercy reaches even the guilty.
The cross of Christ is not merely about pain. It is about exchange.
Your shame for His righteousness. Your guilt for His innocence. Your death sentence for His eternal life.
That is why the resurrection matters.
If Jesus remained dead, Barabbas merely escaped execution temporarily.
But because Christ rose again, freedom became eternal.
The resurrection declared that sin, death, hell, and Satan were defeated.
The empty tomb announced that the substitute was accepted.
And now every person alive faces the same decision the crowd faced that day.
Which Jesus will you choose?
The Jesus shaped by rebellion, pride, politics, self-rule, and human desire?
Or the true Christ who calls people to repentance, surrender, holiness, forgiveness, transformation, and eternal life?
The courtroom scene still echoes through history.
And many are still shouting for Barabbas without realizing it.
But Jesus still stands willing to take the place of the guilty.
Still willing to forgive. Still willing to redeem. Still willing to save.
No matter how dark your past is. No matter how deep your rebellion has been. No matter how chained your soul feels.
The cross proves that mercy is still available.
The cross was built for Barabbas… but Jesus walked toward it anyway.
